slides.title: Pinning third-party files by hash
slides.summary: SRI makes the browser refuse a script or stylesheet whose contents don't match the hash you expected.
body: When you load a script from a CDN, you trust whoever controls that CDN. If it's compromised, every site using it runs the attacker's code.
Subresource Integrity adds an integrity attribute with a cryptographic hash of the file. The browser hashes what it downloads and refuses to run it if the hash doesn't match.

ul: Add crossorigin="anonymous" so the browser can check a cross-origin file.
Pin exact versions in the URL. A floating @latest URL changes, and the hash then blocks it.

body: <mark>SRI only works for files that never change. It suits versioned library builds, not tags that update themselves.</mark>

body.text: The newer Integrity-Policy: blocked-destinations=(script) header makes the browser block any script that has no integrity metadata. Roll it out with Integrity-Policy-Report-Only first. It's newer than SRI itself, so check browser support.
PCI DSS 4.0.1 requirement 6.4.3 asks you to confirm every script on a payment page is unmodified. SRI is one of the simplest ways to show that.

code: curl -s URL | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A

figure.alt: Your HTML pins a script from a CDN with integrity sha384-oqVu… . Top row: the CDN serves the genuine file; the browser computes its SHA-384 hash, it matches the pinned value, and the script runs. Bottom row: the CDN has been compromised and serves a modified file; the computed hash is different, so the browser refuses to run it and reports a network error. A newer Integrity-Policy header can require SRI on every script.
